title: "To make a real impact, we need to become more international"
content: Interview "To make a real impact, we need to become more international" Share article Share link Share on X Elissa Strome leads the Pan-Canadian Artificial Intelligence Strategy at the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CIFAR). Picture CIFAR Elissa Strome of the Canadian Institute for Advanced Research (CIFAR) discusses the opportunities presented by international research collaborations and new geopolitical constellations, as well as how the next generation of researchers can work together. Dr. Strome, you have a black belt in the martial art of taekwondo. Speed and quick reflexes are key in that sport—do these skills help you in your field of research, artificial intelligence? Taekwondo requires two things: discipline and focus. I go to practice three times a week. You have to be disciplined if you want to achieve results. That’s undoubtedly a parallel to advancing research and working with AI. The second parallel is the intense focus required in this sport and in AI—the ability to concentrate, recognize clear opportunities, and block out background noise. And in AI, there’s a lot of noise. Taekwondo is a contact sport. Do you also see the field of AI as a battle arena? It’s an interesting analogy, no question—especially given the current race around AI. But in the realm of research, I don’t like the metaphor of battle and competition. We’re not interested in building the strongest, largest, or most comprehensive AI models; that shouldn’t be an end in itself. So what is your focus? Our goal is to truly understand these systems. Of course, we also want to develop and advance the technology—but in a responsible, strategic way that brings benefits to society. We want to balance technological progress by simultaneously developing an understanding of the risks and mitigating them. This brings us back to our focus: we want to harness the benefits without losing sight of the other challenges. You yourself have been with CIFAR for nine years, working on the delivery of the Pan-Canadian AI strategy. What has happened since then? When I started, universities were still largely working in silos, without much interaction with one another. Since then, we’ve built an interconnected national network anchored by world-class talent from coast to coast. Our three national AI institutes – Amii in Edmonton, Mila in Montreal and the Vector Institute in Toronto – are each building distinct AI ecosystems within their respective regions, but they collaborate seamlessly as part of a unified Canadian strategy. Building on these achievements, what additional benefits do you expect from international collaborations, such as the EU’s initiative for an “Alliance for the Future” with Canada? The challenges are too great for any one country to tackle alone. There are many areas where the EU’s strengths can complement our own, including AI. Germany is a standout example: it has a massive industry with a long tradition of research and development. AI has the potential to make an enormous difference there. In Canada, we have a smaller industrial R&D footprint, but deep foundational AI research. That makes international collaboration a great opportunity for both nations. Could such collaboration also set a precedent in other research areas beyond AI? Let’s take a specific look at Helmholtz: There are already quite a few successful collaborations between CIFAR and various Helmholtz Institutes. At CIFAR, we strive to bring the best people together and build interdisciplinary, international research networks. Helmholtz is highly attractive to talent from all over the world. Research excellence is therefore something that unites us. And both of our organizations have recognized how important international collaboration is—that’s a good sign! Could you be more specific? Which fields are of particular interest for collaborations between Helmholtz and Canada? There’s already a well-established connection in the neurosciences. Data science is another field, and these two areas, in turn, overlap significantly with AI research, which we’ve already discussed. Here’s another example: We’re currently preparing a collaboration with CISPA in the field of cybersecurity. And there’s undoubtedly potential in other fields as well. Here at CIFAR, we have more than a dozen different programs; we’re particularly strong in biomedicine, materials science, and the field of quantum materials—I’m convinced there are good opportunities for collaboration there. Are international research collaborations more important today than they were ten or fifteen years ago? Fifteen years ago, I was at the University of Toronto, and even back then, international partnerships were a priority. Collaboration in science has always helped us find better answers and better train the next generation of researchers.
